native_result.query: At what Socioeconomic levels is the advantage in completion rates for Black students more pronounced?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels indicated by a positive interaction term SES*is_Black(coefficient:0.6271 (significant))
native_result.HypoB: The completion advantage for Black students is concentrated at the high end of the socioeconomic distribution. Raw (unadjusted) Black BA-completion rates are BELOW White rates at every SES stratum (Black 0.44/1.33/1.63/3.03% vs White 1.78/4.32/3.73/3.67% across SES quartiles; overall 1.33% vs 3.54%), so there is no unconditional advantage — but the Black-White gap narrows monotonically with SES (risk ratio 0.25, 0.31, 0.44, 0.83) and reaches statistical parity only in the top SES quartile (SES >= +0.41, ~75th percentile: RD -0.64 pp, 95% CI -2.42 to +2.30, Fisher p=0.72). Once students are compared at equal academic resources (ASVAB composite, class percentile, sex, family size), Black completion exceeds White at every level above the bottom quartile and the advantage grows with SES: adjusted RD -0.01 pp (Q1, RR 0.99), +1.51 (Q2, RR 1.52), +1.76 (Q3, RR 1.62), +3.05 pp (Q4, RR 1.91); the adequately supported pooled upper-SES-half contrast is +2.40 pp (adjusted 5.50% vs 3.10%; 95% bootstrap CI -0.03 to +4.99; RR 1.78, 0.99-2.65). A continuous adjusted-contrast curve crosses zero near SES -1.1 and has a bootstrap CI excluding zero only between SES +0.25 and +1.25 (~68th-94th percentile). Corroborated by a direct within-region adjusted logistic (upper-half OR 1.88, 1.05-3.34, p=0.033), a form-free Mantel-Haenszel OR stratified on ASVAB quintiles (upper-half-SES OR 1.82, 1.02-3.26; bottom-half-SES OR 0.86, 0.44-1.66) and a Firth penalized fit (+2.64 pp upper half, +3.32 pp top quartile). Equivalently, Black completion is far more SES-dependent than White (OR per 1 SD of SES 2.07, 1.47-2.90 vs 1.17, 1.02-1.36; slope difference z=2.99, p=0.003), so high family SES 'buys' much more BA completion for Black students. Hypothesis: the Black advantage in completion rates is most pronounced at upper socioeconomic levels — at and above roughly the 75th percentile of SES (SES >= +0.4 SD, strongest over +0.25 to +1.25) — and is absent at low SES, where Black students remain below White students at every level of resources.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection of structure/coding/missingness and race x SES cross-tabs (inspect_nls_ses.py). 2) stats_lib.py: Wilson, Newcombe hybrid-score RD, Katz RR, Fisher exact; own IRLS logistic (matches statsmodels GLM to 9e-14) and a Jeffreys/Firth penalized logistic whose analytic gradient was verified numerically and whose small-sample bias was benchmarked in simulation. 3) run_analysis.py: unadjusted stratum contrasts (quartiles primary, tertiles/quintiles/extreme-band secondary), adjusted g-computed contrasts from logistic BA ~ SES quartile x Black + Hispanic + ASVAB_z + class-percentile_z + female + family-size_z, 1000x race x SES-stratified bootstrap CIs, within-race SES gradients + trend tests, adjusted Black x SES(z) interaction, Firth sensitivity, common-support and Hispanic-pooling sensitivity. 4) sensitivity_extra.py: adjusted contrast curve over a SES grid (500 bootstraps), covariate-specification ladder, direct within-region models, Mantel-Haenszel/CMH (form-free), relaxed-slope models, ASVAB/SES common support. 5) gradient_test.py: difference of independent within-race logit slopes. 6) verify_with_statsmodels.py: independent re-estimation of every headline number. 7) make_summary.py -> headline_table.csv/md; ANSWER.md. Driver: run_all.sh.

sub_hypo.text: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels, indicated by a significant positive SES*is_Black interaction coefficient of 0.6271.
sub_hypo.context: NLS participants with social background factors and academic resources recorded at secondary school graduation.
sub_hypo.relations: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students increases as SES increases, with a significant positive interaction between SES and Black race status (SES*is_Black coefficient: 0.6271).

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels indicated by a positive interaction term SES*is_Black(coefficient:0.6271 (significant))

sub_hypo.text: Unadjusted Black BA-completion rates are below White rates in every SES quartile, but the relative gap narrows monotonically with SES and reaches statistical parity only in the top quartile.
sub_hypo.context: Black and White NLS participants, grouped by SES quartile; the top quartile begins at SES +0.41, approximately the 75th percentile.
sub_hypo.relations: Black versus White completion rates are 0.44% versus 1.78%, 1.33% versus 4.32%, 1.63% versus 3.73%, and 3.03% versus 3.67% across ascending SES quartiles; overall rates are 1.33% versus 3.54%. Black-to-White risk ratios rise from 0.25 to 0.31 to 0.44 to 0.83. In Q4, the risk difference is -0.64 percentage points (95% CI -2.42 to +2.30; Fisher p=0.72).

sub_hypo.text: At equal measured academic resources and demographic covariates, the Black BA-completion advantage increases with SES, is absent in the bottom quartile, and is most pronounced in the top quartile.
sub_hypo.context: Black–White comparisons among NLS participants within SES quartiles, adjusted for ASVAB composite, class percentile, sex, and family size; the logistic model also includes a Hispanic indicator.
sub_hypo.relations: Adjusted Black-minus-White risk differences increase across Q1–Q4: -0.01, +1.51, +1.76, and +3.05 percentage points, with corresponding risk ratios 0.99, 1.52, 1.62, and 1.91. The stated hypothesis places the strongest advantage at approximately the 75th SES percentile and above (SES >= +0.4 SD) and asserts that Black students remain below White students at low SES at every resource level.

sub_hypo.text: The pooled upper half of SES shows an adjusted Black BA-completion advantage, corroborated by alternative estimation methods.
sub_hypo.context: NLS participants in the upper SES half, comparing Black and White students with adjustment for ASVAB composite, class percentile, sex, and family size; ASVAB-quintile stratification and Firth penalization provide sensitivity checks.
sub_hypo.relations: Upper-half adjusted rates are 5.50% versus 3.10%, a +2.40-percentage-point difference (95% bootstrap CI -0.03 to +4.99), with RR 1.78 (0.99–2.65). A direct within-region adjusted logistic model gives OR 1.88 (1.05–3.34; p=0.033). ASVAB-quintile-stratified Mantel–Haenszel ORs are 1.82 (1.02–3.26) in the upper SES half and 0.86 (0.44–1.66) in the bottom half. Firth estimates are +2.64 percentage points in the upper half and +3.32 in the top quartile.

sub_hypo.text: The continuous adjusted Black–White completion contrast becomes positive near SES -1.1, with a bootstrap confidence interval excluding zero only between SES +0.25 and +1.25.
sub_hypo.context: Black and White NLS participants evaluated over a continuous SES grid, holding measured academic resources and demographic covariates comparable; SES +0.25 to +1.25 corresponds approximately to the 68th–94th percentiles.
sub_hypo.relations: The adjusted Black-minus-White contrast crosses zero near SES -1.1; statistically supported positive contrasts are confined to SES +0.25 through +1.25.

sub_hypo.text: BA completion is more strongly associated with SES among Black students than among White students.
sub_hypo.context: Black and White NLS participants, comparing within-race SES gradients and testing their difference.
sub_hypo.relations: Per one-SD increase in SES, completion odds ratios are 2.07 (95% CI 1.47–2.90) for Black students and 1.17 (1.02–1.36) for White students. The within-race logit-slope difference is significant (z=2.99, p=0.003), indicating a stronger positive SES association for Black students.
